issue_summary:
No regulator anywhere has approved open-source AID (Loop, Trio, iAPS, AndroidAPS, OpenAPS). The pump and the CGM are each approved, but running them together under unapproved software is off-label. Manufacturers therefore disclaim responsibility, and the use may void warranties. That leaves clinicians unsure whether talking about these systems, prescribing the components, or advising on settings exposes them to negligence claims, indemnity problems or professional-conduct risk.

Two 2019 events gave cautious clinicians an official reason to step back. On 17 May 2019 the FDA warned against unauthorized diabetes devices after a single report of an insulin overdose. On 27 June 2019 the FDA issued a safety communication alongside a Class I recall of the Medtronic MiniMed 508 and Paradigm pumps, the same 'loopable' pumps the DIY systems used, because they could be controlled wirelessly by someone nearby.

Professional-body positions have since changed. Early statements said clinicians 'cannot recommend' these systems and users act 'at their own risk': Diabetes Australia (2018), JDRF UK (2019) and Diabetes UK (2020). Later ones say clinicians should support whatever the person chooses: the 2022 Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology international consensus (endorsed by ADCES, ISPAD and IDF), Diabetes Canada (2023), and the ADA Standards of Care (2025). The 2022 ADA/EASD consensus on automated insulin delivery sits between the two. It says regulators and scientific societies do not recommend DIY systems and that liability is 'unsolved', but it still tells clinicians to give safety advice and to document. No country has case law on this, so the chain of liability (regulator, manufacturer, clinic, clinician, developers, user) is still unclear. Clinicians who rely on the older statements or the 2019 warnings may still refuse support or decline to prescribe supplies.
who_is_affected: Adults who loop. Parents and caregivers who build and run systems for children: at least 20% of open-source AID users are 19 or younger, and the law on parental choice here is untested. Endocrinologists and pediatric diabetes teams. Diabetes educators and specialist nurses (DCES/CDCES, DSN). Primary care clinicians who sign supply prescriptions. Hospital and clinic risk managers, indemnity insurers and medical defence organisations. Volunteer open-source developers. Device manufacturers whose pumps and CGMs are used off-label.
system_specificity: All open-source systems, because none is approved. Loop is a partial exception at the algorithm level only. The FDA cleared Tidepool Loop in January 2023, and it ships inside Sequel's twiist AID system (cleared March 2024). DIY Loop builds from LoopKit (for example, on Omnipod DASH with a RileyLink or OrangeLink) are still unapproved. Trio and iAPS (oref algorithm), AndroidAPS and OpenAPS have no cleared version. The 2019 Medtronic recall affected setups on old Medtronic pumps (Loop, OpenAPS and AndroidAPS on 5xx/7xx Paradigm models with old firmware). The 2019 FDA warning described an unauthorized CGM feeding an unauthorized dosing app, which is most relevant to setups using non-iCGM or re-engineered sensor data.
care_setting: Routine adult endocrinology visits and diabetes educator visits; pediatric diabetes clinics, where parental consent and the child's welfare and assent apply; primary care, often when signing pump, pod and sensor prescriptions; pregnancy and obstetric diabetes clinics; inpatient and ED care, where hospital personal-device policies and documentation apply; clinics that specialise in supporting DIY systems and use their own consent and waiver forms (for example BCDiabetes in Canada); and clinic, hospital and insurer risk-management decisions.
trigger_moment: The user first tells the clinic or asks for help starting. Prescription renewals for pods, sensors or a replacement pump, especially an out-of-warranty or recalled Medtronic pump. A clinician being asked to review or change settings. Signing a consent, disclaimer or waiver. An adverse event (severe hypo, DKA, ED or hospital admission), which raises reporting and blame questions. Public warnings and recalls (the FDA warning of May 2019, the Medtronic recall of June 2019). Starting a child on a system. Pregnancy. A change of clinician or clinic policy. Moving to an FDA-cleared system (Tidepool Loop or twiist) or to another commercial AID.

key_sources.title: Braune K, Lal RA, Petruzelkova L, et al. Open-source automated insulin delivery: international consensus statement and practical guidance for health-care professionals. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2022;10(1):58-74
key_sources.country: International (44 health professionals and 4 legal experts from more than 20 countries)
key_sources.sample_size: Expert consensus (n/a); estimated more than 10,000 users worldwide, at least 20% of them aged 19 or younger
key_sources.relevance: The main professional guidance. It says 'regulatory approval does not preclude liability', that no legal precedents exist, and that the chain of accountability is unclear. It supports clinicians discussing open-source AID with competent adults and tells them not to break local law, while asking authorities to clarify or update the law. Panel 3 sets safe practice under four headings: discuss approved options; keep prescribing regulated devices so users stay eligible for reimbursement; document discussions with a disclaimer (system unregulated, the clinic takes no responsibility, data handling may not meet data-protection rules); report adverse events. It recommends iCGM-grade sensors because of the FDA warning, and asks manufacturers to allow secure remote commands on in-warranty pumps. Endorsed by ADCES, ISPAD, IDF Global, IDF Europe, the ABCD Diabetes Technology Network, the German Association of Diabetes Educators, the Danish Endocrine Society, the Danish Diabetes Nursing Association and the Czech Diabetes Society.

key_sources.title: US FDA press announcement: FDA warns against use of unauthorized devices for diabetes management
key_sources.sample_size: 1 adverse-event report (insulin overdose needing medical treatment; it happened outside the US, the patient recovered, and the cause was not established)
key_sources.relevance: The FDA's first warning touching DIY systems. It told patients to use only devices the agency has reviewed and to report problems to MedWatch. It gave no specific guidance to clinicians. Diabetes Canada's 2023 clinician guide names FDA warnings, together with the ADA standards of that time, as reinforcing clinicians' reluctance to support DIY AID.

key_sources.title: FDA safety communication and Medtronic Class I recall: MiniMed 508 and MiniMed Paradigm insulin pumps, cybersecurity risk (as reported in the FDA press release copy and trade press)
key_sources.year: 2019 (27 June); recall extended to the matching remote controllers in Oct 2021
key_sources.sample_size: About 4,000 US patients identified at the time; FDA aware of no confirmed patient harm
key_sources.relevance: Someone nearby could wirelessly change settings or deliver insulin. The pumps cannot be patched, so patients were steered to newer pumps. These were the 'loopable' pumps the DIY systems relied on, which lets clinicians argue against supporting or supplying them. Community commentary at the time saw the recall as Medtronic taking back loopable pumps (community anecdote, Sophos Naked Security 2019; not checked against primary sources). The 2022 consensus answers with a call for secure remote-command access on modern in-warranty pumps.

key_sources.title: JDRF (now Breakthrough T1D) statement on FDA safety warning for DIY systems (A. Kowalski)
key_sources.relevance: Called the warning 'not unexpected'. Asked the community to report problems and said each person should weigh the risks and benefits themselves. Backed FDA-reviewed versions of DIY approaches and the Open Protocol AID initiative launched in 2017. In 2023 JDRF welcomed the Tidepool Loop clearance as a step toward open protocol. No current US Breakthrough T1D position statement specifically on DIY systems was found.

key_sources.title: JDRF UK (Breakthrough T1D UK) position statement on type 1 diabetes 'DIY' technologies
key_sources.sample_size: Estimated more than 100 UK users at the time
key_sources.relevance: Cannot endorse unregulated systems but respects people's right to choose. Calls for 'enhanced legal and reputational protection' for clinicians, says a patient's offer of an indemnity letter is not a solution, and calls for funded training and protected time. Notes the MHRA has no jurisdiction over individuals and that off-label use can void warranties.

key_sources.title: Diabetes UK: Do it yourself (DIY) closed loop for people living with type 1 diabetes, position statement
key_sources.year: 2020 (15 Jan); page says it is under review, with a revision expected early 2027
key_sources.relevance: Users 'should continue to get support and care from their diabetes team', but health professionals 'cannot recommend their use', and users act 'at their own risk'. Endorsed by the Royal College of Nursing (per secondary sources). Diabetes UK endorses participation in the ABCD DIY APS audit as best practice.

key_sources.title: Diabetes Australia position statement: People with type 1 diabetes and Do It Yourself (DIY) technology solutions
key_sources.year: 2018 (22 Aug); no newer DIY-specific statement found
key_sources.sample_size: Estimated about 100 Australian users at the time
key_sources.relevance: Does not endorse these systems; calls them 'highly experimental', not TGA-approved and used at the person's own risk. Lists 'medico-legal risks and issues with registration and practice' as clinicians' concerns. Says clinicians cannot recommend the systems but users must keep receiving care. Notes that ADS and ADEA were developing advice for clinicians. Later Diabetes Australia work (2024) focuses on access to commercial AID.

key_sources.title: Diabetes Canada Clinical Practice Guidelines Expert Working Group (Halperin IJ, Chambers A, Covello L, Farnsworth K, Morrison AE, Schuklenk U, Witteman HO, Senior P). Do-It-Yourself Automated Insulin Delivery: A Position Statement. Can J Diabetes 2023;47(5):381-388; with A Health-care Practitioner User's Guide, 389-397
key_sources.relevance: Clinicians should support people with T1D in whichever insulin-delivery method they choose and should discuss AID, both commercial and DIY, with everyone with T1D. It calls refusing to support DIY users gatekeeping that effectively denies equitable access, and warns of clinician bias about who 'suits' AID (education, cognitive ability). Names the lack of regulatory approval, 'exacerbated by' the ADA standards and FDA warnings, as a barrier, and notes that some clinicians feel threatened when the patient is the expert. The user's guide covers Loop, AndroidAPS and OpenAPS and offers a CARES-based framework. Details are from secondary summaries; the full text is paywalled. [uncertain]

key_sources.title: Sherr JL, Heinemann L, Fleming GA, et al. Automated insulin delivery: benefits, challenges, and recommendations. ADA/EASD Joint Diabetes Technology Working Group consensus report. Diabetes Care 2022;45:3058-3074 / Diabetologia 2023;66:3-22
key_sources.relevance: Says DIY AID is 'not recommended by regulatory agencies or scientific societies' because of evidence gaps and 'unsolved liability issues'. If asked, the clinician should say: the system is unapproved and used off-label, so the component manufacturers are not liable; the clinician cannot prescribe it; and the patient takes responsibility. The clinician can still advise on safety, help with a backup plan, and document and report problems in the EHR. Technical questions go to the DIY community, not the clinician. It calls the liability question 'exponentially larger' for DIY systems.

key_sources.title: American Diabetes Association. 7. Diabetes Technology: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2025. Diabetes Care 2025;48(Suppl 1):S146-S166 (recommendation 7.29); 2026 update
key_sources.relevance: Per secondary sources: recommendation 7.29 tells clinicians to support people who choose an open-source closed-loop system and give them diabetes management advice. It adopts 'open-source' or OS-AID in place of 'DIY' and notes that open code gives clinicians a fuller view of risks and benefits. Commentators read this as a reversal of earlier discouragement. The exact wording and evidence grade were not verified against the primary text, which was paywalled or blocked. [uncertain]

key_sources.title: Crabtree TSJ, Choudhary P, Hammond P, Lumb A, McLay A, Wilmot EG. Health-care professional opinions of DIY artificial pancreas systems in the UK. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2020;8:186-187 (DTN-UK national survey 2019; ABCD poster)
key_sources.relevance: Most would not start conversations about DIY APS: 67% cited non-regulation, 63% limited knowledge and 32% professional indemnity. 59% were not comfortable providing clinical support. 13% (41/317) said they would stop supplying consumables. Only 2% saw the systems as dangerous. 97% said HCPs should learn more, and 47% would use one if they had T1D.

key_sources.title: Morrison AE et al. Canadian Healthcare Providers' Attitudes Towards Automated Insulin Delivery Systems (medRxiv preprint; cited in Diabetes Canada 2023)
key_sources.relevance: Respondents reported more barriers to DIY than to commercial AID (p=0.001), mainly unfamiliarity and medico-legal risk. A secondary summary of the Diabetes Canada statement says 73% felt able to support commercial AID users but only 22% DIY users. [uncertain: percentages from a secondary summary]

key_sources.title: Raimond LH, O'Donnell S, Boggild-Damkvist T, Filges T, Lomborg K. Open-source automated insulin delivery systems and formal healthcare: a qualitative study of challenges in the interaction between service-users with type 1 diabetes and healthcare professionals. Chronic Illness 2023;19(4):836-847
key_sources.relevance: Users are 'reticent about disclosing' their systems to clinicians. Guidelines can reduce clinicians' legal responsibility, but unclear ethical responsibility remains a barrier to meaningful clinical interaction.

key_sources.title: Dickson R, Bell J, Dar A, Downey L, Moore V, Quigley M. #WeAreNotWaiting: DIY artificial pancreas systems and challenges for the law. Diabetic Medicine 2022;39(5):e14715
key_sources.relevance: Liability is unclear because many parties are involved. Clinicians' duties fall mainly under negligence law. Discussing the systems is not prescribing. Withholding prescriptions from someone already looping could itself be negligent if it causes harm. Manufacturers can rely on warnings against off-label use. Open-source software fits product-liability law poorly. Parental discretion for children is legally untested.

key_sources.title: Roberts J, Moore V, Quigley M. Prescribing unapproved medical devices? The case of DIY artificial pancreas systems. Medical Law International 2021;21(1):42-68
key_sources.relevance: Argues that nothing in GMC guidance stops clinicians from starting discussions about DIY APS, and that in some cases it may require them to. The guidance urges caution before prescribing unapproved devices but does not forbid it.

key_sources.title: Moore V, Quigley M. Can clinicians be held liable for caring for OS AID users? (Everyday Cyborgs blog, summarising a chapter in Patient Safety Law, Ethics and Practice in the NHS, Routledge 2026)
key_sources.relevance: Calls clinician negligence liability 'highly unlikely' when clinicians discuss the systems, advise accurately, or prescribe licensed components in line with NICE (analysed under Bolam/Bolitho, Montgomery and McCulloch 2023). The user's own setup choices probably break the chain of causation. The main risk is a negligent misstatement about technical details. It says clinician anxiety that drives a hands-off approach is 'not well-founded in law'.

key_sources.title: Healio/Endocrine Today: As DIY 'loopers' reinvent artificial pancreas, endocrinologists confront safety, liability concerns
key_sources.relevance: Captures US clinician views before the 2019 warnings. Peters (USC): the pump and sensor are approved but the algorithm is not; support capable patients and refer on if uncomfortable. Hamdy (Joslin): does not advise building one but keeps seeing these patients. Pettus (UCSD): worries that liability fears will push patients away. Lias (FDA): not designed in a quality system. Barnard: prescribing an unauthorized treatment is a 'clear-cut violation', and anyone who sets up a system for someone else may be liable. Medtronic 'strongly discourage[s]' device modification.

key_sources.title: Healio: For DIY loopers, diabetes educators play important role (AADE 2018 session)
key_sources.relevance: Describes outright refusals by clinicians and educators ('Absolutely not, I will not support you in this'). Refused patients often look for a new doctor or educator, and community groups advise them to 'find someone who will help you'.

key_sources.title: BCDiabetes: Looping with BCDiabetes, Informed Consent and Waiver for Adults (and a Minor version)
key_sources.sample_size: 2,479 people supported (Loop 2,022; AndroidAPS 362; iAPS 73; Trio 22). In the first 1,442 with outcome data: 0 deaths, 4 DKA, 14 patient-reported severe hypos; TIR rose from 60% to 73%.
key_sources.relevance: A real clinic model of documented risk transfer. It explains off-label use, says the clinic 'cannot recommend' DIY systems, and says liability is unclear if something fails. The patient assumes full responsibility and gives a broad release of claims. The form discloses that the clinic is paid for installing and supporting the systems (a conflict of interest). It covers TestFlight distribution and expiry, a fallback to the Omnipod PDM or MDI, and data-sharing consent. Outcome data are self-reported by a clinic with a financial interest.

key_sources.title: O'Donnell S, Cooper D, Chen Y, et al. Barriers to uptake of open-source automated insulin delivery systems: OPEN survey. Diabetes Res Clin Pract 2023;197:110235
key_sources.relevance: Fear of losing healthcare-provider support was one of four major barriers to starting, along with sourcing components, confidence in technical skills, and time and energy.

key_sources.title: Crabtree TSJ, Ryder REJ, Wilmot EG. #WeAreNotWaiting: Do-It-Yourself Artificial Pancreas Systems: the story so far. Br J Diabetes 2022;22(Suppl 1):S82-S84
key_sources.sample_size: Review; ABCD DIY APS audit with more than 100 UK users
key_sources.relevance: Says UK services were inconsistent and GMC guidance unclear. Advises clinicians to start discussions with full information, explain the risks of out-of-warranty equipment, keep supplying NHS pumps and CGM, and join the ABCD audit. Users worried more about a negative response from their team than about regulation.

key_sources.title: Tidepool: FDA clearance of Tidepool Loop; Sequel twiist AID system 510(k) clearance
key_sources.sample_size: Clearance supported by observational real-world Loop data (BCDiabetes cites 873 Loopers; Lum et al. 2021 reported 558) [uncertain]
key_sources.relevance: The first regulatory clearance of an open-source-derived algorithm. It creates a prescribable path for the Loop algorithm (twiist only) but leaves DIY builds unapproved. Opponents can now argue DIY is unnecessary given 'four approved systems' (Forlenza, ADA 2023 debate, STAT, June 2023).

key_sources.title: Diabetes Voice (IDF): DIY artificial pancreas gets warning from FDA
key_sources.relevance: DIY developers issued a joint statement through the Looped group and OpenAPS asking users to 'report adverse events on DIY systems, if and when they occur'. This shows the community's response to the warning was transparency rather than avoidance.

evidence_strength: Mostly professional guidance and expert legal opinion. Position statements, consensus reports and guidelines exist from the international consensus (2022), ADA/EASD (2022), Diabetes Canada (2023), the ADA Standards (2025), Diabetes UK (2020), Diabetes Australia (2018) and JDRF UK (2019). Peer-reviewed legal analyses come from the UK (Roberts 2021, Dickson 2022, Moore and Quigley 2026). Clinician attitudes are documented in two HCP surveys (UK n=317 in 2019; Canada n=204 in 2021) and small qualitative studies (Raimond 2023: 5 users, 6 HCPs). The regulatory triggers are official FDA communications. Evidence that those triggers caused clinician pushback is indirect: guideline authors cite them as barriers, alongside news coverage and community anecdote. No case law exists anywhere.
prevalence_or_magnitude: Users: the 2021 consensus estimated more than 10,000 worldwide, at least 20% of them aged 19 or younger. One Canadian clinic (BCDiabetes) alone had supported 2,479 people by July 2025. Clinicians, UK 2019 (n=317): 67% would not start conversations because the systems are unregulated, 63% cited limited knowledge, 32% indemnity concerns, 59% were uncomfortable providing support, and 13% would stop supplying consumables, but only 2% called the systems dangerous and 97% wanted more training. Clinicians, Canada 2021 (n=204): more barriers reported for DIY than for commercial AID (p=0.001), with medico-legal risk prominent; a secondary summary reports 73% able to support commercial AID users versus 22% for DIY [uncertain]. A 2021 UK interview study (n=20 HCPs) found 19 named liability uncertainty and 19 the lack of formal guidelines as the main barriers [uncertain: conference abstract seen only through search snippets]. Regulatory events: one adverse-event report behind the FDA warning (May 2019); about 4,000 US patients identified in the Medtronic 508/Paradigm recall (June 2019), with no confirmed harm. Professional bodies: at least 9 organisations endorsed the 2022 consensus, including ADCES, ISPAD and IDF. Diabetes UK, Diabetes Australia and JDRF UK statements still say 'cannot recommend' or 'at own risk', and the Diabetes UK revision is not expected until early 2027. Litigation: no known lawsuits or case law in any jurisdiction (consensus 2021; Moore and Quigley 2026).
data_quality_caveats: HCP surveys are from 2019-2021. They predate the Tidepool Loop clearance (2023), Diabetes Canada (2023) and the ADA 2025 change, so current attitudes may be more supportive. Survey respondents are self-selected technology-network members, which likely overstates interest. Legal analyses are UK-only, and none is US-specific. The single report behind the FDA warning involved a non-US patient and an unclear cause. The Medtronic recall reported no confirmed harm. Some figures come from secondary summaries (Canadian 73% vs 22%; the ADA 2025 recommendation wording), not primary text. BCDiabetes outcomes are self-reported by a clinic with a declared financial interest. Several professional statements are old and unrevised (Diabetes Australia 2018, JDRF UK 2019, Diabetes UK 2020).
clinician_perspective:
What clinicians fear:
(1) Legal and professional exposure: indemnity (32% in the UK 2019 survey), 'medico-legal risks and issues with registration and practice' (Diabetes Australia 2018), and the claim that prescribing an unauthorized treatment is a violation (Barnard, 2018).
(2) Endorsing something unregulated: 67% gave non-regulation as the reason they would not raise DIY APS. The FDA (Lias, 2018) said the systems were 'not designed in a quality system'.
(3) Not knowing enough to advise safely: 63% limited knowledge, and 59% uncomfortable giving clinical support or troubleshooting.
(4) Unclear ethical responsibility even when legal guidance exists (Raimond 2023).
(5) Growing technical demands and less control when the patient is the expert. Diabetes Canada notes some clinicians 'feel threatened' by this role reversal.
(6) Hardware risk: out-of-warranty or second-hand pumps, recalled Medtronic models, and non-iCGM sensors (named in the 2019 warnings).
(7) Since 2023 a newer objection: DIY is unnecessary now that cleared systems exist (Forlenza, ADA 2023 debate).

What guidance and legal scholars answer: liability is 'highly unlikely' if clinicians give accurate information, admit what they do not know, and keep prescribing licensed components (Moore and Quigley 2026). Withholding prescriptions from an existing looper could itself be negligent (Dickson 2022). GMC guidance does not bar starting discussions (Roberts 2021). The ADA/EASD consensus says clinicians can advise on safety and backup plans, and should document.

What clinicians say they need: clear legal and professional guidance (19 of 20 in UK interviews), protected and funded training time (JDRF UK; 97% want to learn more), simple documentation and disclaimer templates (consensus panel 3), a referral route to experienced colleagues (consensus recommendation 5), and a way to know exactly which system and settings a patient is running before advising.
effect_on_relationship:
Legal and regulatory uncertainty is the main reason clinicians take a defensive stance, and that stance changes what patients disclose. Documented reactions range from flat refusal ('Absolutely not, I will not support you in this'; AADE 2018) to threats to stop supplies (13% of UK HCPs would) to quietly referring the patient elsewhere. Patients respond by hiding their use: users are 'reticent about disclosing' (Raimond 2023), and fear of losing provider support is a major barrier for would-be users (O'Donnell 2023, n=129). Others find a more accommodating clinician, or lean on the peer community for all technical and settings advice, which shrinks the clinic's role to supply prescriptions.

The 2019 FDA warning and the Medtronic recall gave skeptical clinicians an official reference to cite. They also strengthened a patient narrative of institutions against users: some community comments read the recall as reclaiming loopable pumps [uncertain: community anecdote].

Formal documentation can either build or erode trust. Consensus-style disclaimers and documented discussions let a clinician stay engaged without endorsing the system. Heavy waivers, such as BCDiabetes' broad release of claims including for death, make the arrangement explicit but put almost all risk on the patient.

Where newer guidance is adopted (the 2022 consensus, Diabetes Canada 2023, ADA 2025), the relationship can become shared care. The clinician owns safety advice, backup planning, reviewing glucose data and prescribing components. The user owns the system and the technical configuration. Patients can now point clinicians to these citations, which shifts the burden of justification onto clinicians who refuse.
decision_ownership: Today: the user, or a parent for a child, decides to build and run the system, and in practice owns every setting. All major guidance places responsibility on the user. The ADA/EASD consensus says the patient 'assumes responsibility', component manufacturers are not liable for off-label use, and the clinician cannot prescribe the system itself. Clinicians decide whether to discuss it, whether to keep prescribing components (the consensus says they should, to keep users eligible for reimbursement), whether to give settings advice, and what to document. Peers and developers often decide settings in practice but carry no formal duty. Liability is unresolved: the consensus lists regulators, manufacturers, institutions, clinicians, developers and users as possible links in the chain, with no precedent. UK legal analysis expects a user's own configuration choices to break causation, with contributory negligence or 'volenti' (acceptance of a known risk) possibly applying, which leaves clinicians exposed mainly for negligent misstatements. Some clinics move risk by contract, using a consent form plus a release. Product liability for open-source software is untested.
disclosure_risk: High. Clinicians who cite 'cannot recommend', unregulated status or the 2019 FDA warning can withhold supplies (13% of UK HCPs said they would), refuse support or discharge patients. So users have a reason to hide looping, share only CGM summaries, or describe themselves simply as pump plus CGM users. Fear of losing provider support deters adoption (OPEN survey 2023), and users are reluctant to disclose (Raimond 2023). The risk falls where a clinic uses newer guidance or offers a written disclaimer that frames disclosure as safe. Sharing data through Tidepool labels uploads 'DIY Loop', which reveals the system.
regulatory_status_dependency: Strongly dependent. With an FDA-cleared system (Tidepool Loop inside the twiist AID system, cleared March 2024), the algorithm becomes a prescribable, labelled device. The off-label argument disappears, manufacturer support and complaint handling exist, and clinicians are covered by normal standard-of-care rules, so most of this issue goes away for twiist users. It does not change anything for DIY Loop on Omnipod or old Medtronic pumps, for Trio, iAPS, AndroidAPS or OpenAPS, or for countries without a cleared equivalent. Twiist's commercial availability and US-only scope limit how many people it helps [uncertain: launch timing reported as limited 2025, national about 2026]. The cleared option also gives skeptical clinicians a new argument that DIY is no longer needed.
workarounds:
Users: bring copies of the 2022 Lancet consensus, the Diabetes Canada 2023 statement or the ADA 2025 recommendation to appointments. Use LoopDocs/LoopTips 'endocrinologist and Loop' pages to frame the conversation. Ask for prescriptions for the approved components only (pods, sensors), and keep a backup plan (PDM or MDI). Switch to a clinician known to support DIY users, often found through Facebook groups. Avoid disclosure when they expect hostility. Some move to cleared systems (Omnipod 5, Control-IQ, twiist) to end the conflict.

Clinicians: follow consensus panel 3 (discuss approved options, document the discussion with a disclaimer, keep prescribing components, report adverse events), or the ADA/EASD script (state that the system is off-label, the patient is responsible, and the clinician will advise on safety and backup). Refer to experienced colleagues. Some clinics use written informed consent and waivers (BCDiabetes, with a paid installation and support service). UK services take part in the ABCD DIY APS audit, which Diabetes UK endorses as best practice.

Community: developers' joint statement encouraging adverse-event reporting (2019); recommendations to use iCGM sensors and in-warranty pumps.
existing_tools: Guidance documents: the 2022 Lancet consensus panel 3, with its disclaimer elements; the Diabetes Canada 2023 user's guide (CARES framework); ADCES DANAtech open-source AID modules; LoopDocs and LoopTips clinician pages. Consent tools: clinic-specific consent and waiver forms (BCDiabetes, delivered through Smartwaiver). Adverse-event reporting: FDA MedWatch, MHRA Yellow Card, Health Canada, plus developer issue trackers on GitHub and Discord. Registries: the ABCD DIY APS audit (UK) and the OPEN project surveys. Data platforms: Tidepool clinic workspace (labels uploads 'DIY Loop'; settings history for Loop 3.2+) and Nightscout (patient-hosted, read-only token sharing). Clinic EHRs hold free-text documentation of the discussion. None of these was built for liability or regulatory management. [uncertain: no purpose-built tool for recording consent and the split of responsibility in DIY AID was found]
existing_tool_coverage_gap: No tool records who proposed, approved and applied each settings change, so clinician advice and user action cannot be told apart afterwards. No standard, jurisdiction-aware disclaimer or consent record links to the data the clinician reviewed. Nothing captures system identity at the time of advice (app and version, algorithm, pump model, firmware and warranty status, CGM type and whether it is iCGM), which is what the warnings and the recall turned on. There is no single adverse-event report that reaches the clinic, the developers and the regulator together. Nothing gives clinicians a current, citable summary of professional-body positions to replace outdated 2019-era references. Nightscout data handling may not meet HIPAA or GDPR expectations, a risk the consensus disclaimer itself flags. Tidepool shows data but nothing about consent or responsibility.
data_artifacts_involved: Signed consent or disclaimer, and documentation of the discussion in the EHR. A system identity record (app and build version, algorithm, pump model and firmware, warranty or recall status, CGM model and iCGM status). Settings snapshot and change history with who made each change. Clinician recommendation log. Override and temp-basal logs around adverse events. Adverse-event reports (MedWatch, Yellow Card) and app issue reports. Component prescriptions. Data-sharing consent records.
implication_for_collaboration_tool:
1) Built-in responsibility record. Offer a jurisdiction-aware acknowledgement modelled on consensus panel 3 (system unregulated; the clinic takes no responsibility for the software; data handling caveats; the user's ongoing duty to self-educate). The user acknowledges it once, it is dated and versioned, and it exports as a PDF for the EHR. Do not present it as a liability waiver; leave waivers to clinics' own lawyers.

2) Attribution on every settings change. Mark each change as proposed by the clinician, a peer or the user; record whether it was accepted or edited; and log who applied it in the app, with timestamps. Clinicians should only suggest. The user must always apply changes in their own app. The tool should never write to the device, which keeps the clinician in an advisory role and avoids the tool becoming part of the dosing system.

3) System identity card shown at every review: app name, version and build date; algorithm (Loop, oref/Trio/iAPS, AAPS); pump model, firmware and warranty status; CGM source. Flag recalled Medtronic 508/Paradigm pumps and non-iCGM or re-engineered sensor sources, because those were what the 2019 warnings targeted.

4) Adverse-event workflow: one structured report (event, glucose and insulin data window, settings at the time) that the user can send to the clinic, file with the developers, and use to prefill MedWatch, Yellow Card or Health Canada. This meets the consensus and ADA/EASD reporting duty.

5) A clinician brief page with a one-screen, dated summary of current positions and legal analysis (consensus panel 3, ADA/EASD 'what to tell the patient', ADA 2025 recommendation 7.29, Diabetes Canada 2023, UK legal view that liability is 'highly unlikely' when advice is accurate and documented), plus where each regional body still says 'cannot recommend'. Keep it up to date; Diabetes UK is revising its statement for 2027.

6) A safe-disclosure path: let users share a 'what I run and what I accept' summary before the visit, so disclosure is framed and the clinic can choose how to engage. Include a directory or referral route to experienced clinicians.

7) Treat FDA-cleared Tidepool Loop and twiist users in the same workflow but labelled 'regulated', so the tool does not depend on DIY status and supports migration.

8) Pay attention to the product's own regulatory status. Sharing data and recording messages is low-risk. Generating specific dosing recommendations for clinicians could be regulated as clinical decision support or a medical device. Get regulatory and legal review before adding automated settings suggestions [uncertain]. Store data under HIPAA and GDPR-grade controls; the consensus disclaimer flags data protection as a known gap.
severity_rank: High: legal and regulatory uncertainty decides whether a clinician engages at all (59% uncomfortable supporting, 13% would stop supplies, UK 2019), and that drives patients to hide their use and turn to peers.
safety_criticality: Medium-high, indirect. Liability fear does not cause harm directly. It does produce unsupervised use, hidden use (so inpatient and ED teams may not know a closed loop is running), unreported adverse events, and reliance on out-of-warranty or recalled pumps. The underlying regulatory triggers were real hazards: an insulin overdose from an unauthorized CGM-plus-dosing combination (FDA, 2019) and a wireless over- or under-delivery vulnerability (Medtronic recall, 2019; no confirmed harm). [uncertain: no study links clinician refusal to measured adverse outcomes]
equity_impact: Hardest hit, mostly by inference [uncertain]: people in places where the only local or covered specialist refuses DIY support (rural areas, single-clinic regions, closed health plans), who cannot shop for another clinician. Children and adolescents, whose parents' legal standing to choose DIY is untested and who face extra clinician caution. People in countries with outdated or restrictive positions (Australia 2018, UK 2020 statements still current) or with no cleared alternative. AndroidAPS, Trio and iAPS users, who have no regulated equivalent like twiist. Low-income users who rely on out-of-warranty or second-hand pumps, which guidance warns against. People judged by clinicians as less educated or less capable, whom Diabetes Canada warns are subject to gatekeeping bias. Non-English speakers, who have less access to the English-language guidance needed to persuade clinicians.
